body: Hallucinated numbers are the practical danger. In FinanceBench (2023-era models), **GPT-4 Turbo with retrieval failed 81% of questions about filings**. Long-context runs failed 21% (GPT-4 Turbo) and 24% (Claude 2) ([Patronus/PR Newswire](https://prnewswire.com/news-releases/patronus-ai-launches-industry-first-llm-benchmark-for-finance-to-address-hallucinations-301990858.html)). Current frontier models are likely better, but no 2026 benchmark figure was found. Indian guides warn that plain chatbots give stale or invented numbers for Indian companies, and recommend pasting or connecting Screener data instead ([LumiChats](https://lumichats.com/blog/ai-for-stock-market-investing-india-2026)). The defensible role for AI is therefore as an **analyst-productivity multiplier**. It reads, summarises, compares, red-teams and flags forensic issues in primary documents that you supply. It should not be an oracle that tells you what will go up.

body:
The table below sets out what the research found for each name in your list. In almost every case the advantage came from circumstance (era, capital size, network, structure) as much as from insight, and much of it has since been competed away or regulated out.

| Winner | The real edge | Capital and leverage structure | Can you replicate it today? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Young Buffett (1950–69) | Exhaustive reading of obscure securities. Field checks. Tiny capital in an unscreened market | ~$9,800 personal savings, then $105,100 partnership with no management fee | The work ethic, yes. The 1950s net-net universe, no: screens now find them in seconds |
| Berkshire Buffett (1970s–) | Cheap, safe, quality stocks held for decades | ~1.7x leverage via insurance float costing ~3 points below T-bills | No. Broker margin is costly and callable |
| Peter Lynch (1977–90) | Industrial-scale legwork, pre-Reg FD management access, small starting fund | ~$20M fund, closed to new money until 1981 | Partly: the legwork on a handful of companies |
| R K Damani | Broker-family network, 1992 bear trades, then founding D-Mart | Founder stake of ~67–82% in Avenue Supermarts | The business-building lesson, yes. The network and era, no |
| Rakesh Jhunjhunwala | Trading skill, borrowed early capital, being bearish in 1992, then one huge concentrated holding (Titan) | ₹5,000 seed plus money from his brother's clients | The holding-through-pessimism lesson only |
| Porinju Veliyath | Early discovery of neglected small caps. His own following moves prices | Fee-earning PMS (2% fixed plus 10% over a 10% hurdle) | Partly, if you can survive a −67% two-year drawdown |
| P R Sundar | Option-selling style plus a large audience | Most verifiable income was advisory fees | No. Retail loss rates in options are about 88–93% |
| Jane Street and prop desks | Speed, scale, balance sheet, order-flow visibility | Billions in risk capital, member-level costs | No |

body: SEBI's settlement order of 25 May 2023 found that Sundar's Mansun Consultancy had collected about ₹4.6 crore in unregistered advisory fees, via daily Telegram trade calls sold on his blog. The order is from 2023, not 2024 as the brief assumed. Sundar, his wife and the company settled without admitting or denying the findings. They disgorged ₹6,07,69,863 (fees plus 12% interest), paid ₹15.6 lakh each (₹46.8 lakh total), and agreed to a one-year bar from dealing in securities. His method, selling Nifty/Bank Nifty and stock options for theta, earns steady premium with fat-tail losses. SEBI's F&O studies show about 91% of individual F&O traders lose money.

body:
`case_study:cox-and-kings-2019` | 2019-06-26 | tickers: COX&KINGS | confidence: single-source

Cox & Kings, a 250-year-old travel brand, defaulted on commercial paper on 26 Jun 2019; the stock fell sharply within two days and went to ~Rs 2-3 from ~Rs 250-400 levels of 2015-18. Lenders' claims ~Rs 5,500 cr in insolvency. A lender-appointed PwC audit found ~Rs 4,367 cr siphoned and books manipulated from Apr 2014 to Jun 2019 to obtain bank credit; foreign subsidiaries (e.g., Prometheon) allegedly forged reports of global audit firms and bank statements, which were then consolidated by Indian auditors. Visible flags: (1) a 'travel' business that should be working-capital-positive carried heavy and rising debt; (2) large receivables and loans/advances despite customers paying in advance; (3) CFO persistently weak relative to reported profit; (4) debt-funded 2011 Holidaybreak (UK) acquisition and complex offshore holding chains; (5) consolidated accounts relying on subsidiaries audited by other firms; (6) high promoter pledges and dependence on CP and Yes Bank lending. Lesson: when a business model implies negative working capital but the balance sheet shows high receivables and debt, the accounts are wrong. Offshore subsidiaries audited by different firms are a soft spot in consolidation.

**Lesson:** Business model should predict the working-capital sign; mismatch = red flag
**Spotted early by:** forensic forum posters (ValuePickr), CP market

`insight:great-business-crash` · confidence: verified

Every long-run winner in this library had at least one deep drawdown: Amazon -94% (1999-2001), Booking -99% (2000-02), MercadoLibre ~-88% (2008) and ~-67% (2021-22), Netflix ~-80% (2011-12) and -76% (2021-22), Shopify -87% (2022), Meta -77% (2021-22), Palantir -87% (2021-22), Apple -61% (2007-09) and -44% (2012-13), Microsoft -37% (2022), AMD -67% (2021-22), TSMC -58% (2022), ASML -59% (2021-22). Recovery signal that was visible at the bottom in the cases that recovered: core engagement/usage metrics kept growing (Netflix streaming hours, Meta daily users, MELI payments volume) and the cause was management choices or macro, not loss of the moat; management then made a visible reversal (Netflix dropping Qwikster, Meta's efficiency cuts, Shopify selling logistics). Non-recoveries in this set (SMCI, Enphase, Novo so far) had moat or governance problems instead: commodity margins, subsidy-dependent demand, or a superior competitor. Practical rules: size positions so a -75% move is survivable (see strategy:position-sizing); write down in advance which usage metric would prove the business, not the stock, is broken.

body:
`person:john-templeton` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: global, us, process, contrarian, base-rate

Pioneer of global investing. Folklore-grade but widely repeated: in Sept 1939, at the outbreak of WWII, he borrowed $10,000 and bought 100 shares of every NYSE stock trading under $1 (~104 companies, ~34 in bankruptcy) and sold ~4 years later for roughly 4x (details unverified in this research). Templeton Growth Fund (1954-1992): $10,000 grew to ~$2m by 1992, ~13.96% annualised per one source (14.5% often quoted, unverified). Structural edge: early access to cheap foreign markets - he bought Japan in the 1960s at P/E ~3-4x when few Westerners did. Process: 'the time of maximum pessimism is the best time to buy'; compare price with value across every country and industry; buy the cheapest relative to long-term earnings power; diversify widely. His cycle line: 'bull markets are born on pessimism, grow on skepticism, mature on optimism and die on euphoria.' Mistakes: exited Japan years before its 1989 peak (early, missed the final leg); a diversified value approach lags in growth-led eras. 1999-2000 he reportedly shorted Nasdaq IPOs around lock-up expiries (unverified). Copyable: keep a global/sector 'cheapest vs own history' list and act when news is worst; diversify bargain baskets rather than betting on one distressed name; use his pessimism-to-euphoria ladder as a cycle checklist.

| key | value |
|---|---|
| signature_trades | 1939 sub-$1 basket (folklore, ~4x); Japan 1960s |
| track_record | TGF ~14%/yr 1954-1992 (single-source) |
| mistakes | left Japan too early |
| copyable | max-pessimism buying, cheap-vs-history global screen |

`person:group-mahindra` · flag: **clean** · confidence: verified · tickers: M&M, M&MFIN, TECHM, MAHLIFE, MHRIL, MAHLOG, SWARAJENG

Flag: CLEAN. Promoter Mahindra family (Anand Mahindra, chairman) with professional management; Anish Shah became the first non-family group CEO/MD (2021). Listed: Mahindra & Mahindra, Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services, Tech Mahindra, Mahindra Lifespace, Mahindra Holidays, Mahindra Logistics, Swaraj Engines (and others). No promoter pledging; dividends regular. The defining governance positive is the 2020-21 capital-allocation reset: the board rejected a ~$406 m fresh equity infusion into loss-making SsangYong (Apr-2020), and the group exited or shut SsangYong (sold to KG group 2022-23), GenZe, GippsAero and others -- ~15 underperforming businesses per a 2026 report (single-source). Tech Mahindra's 2009 rescue of fraud-hit Satyam is a legacy positive. Blemishes: past value destruction from the 2010 SsangYong purchase and international ventures; Mahindra Finance faced an RBI bar on outsourced recovery (Sep-2022, lifted Dec-2022) and a ~Rs 150 cr fraud at a Mizoram branch (2023, unverified magnitude). Status Nov-2026: no open governance issues found; the group is a reference case for 'killing losers' discipline.

- **red flags:** legacy international losses; M&M Finance operational lapses
- **good conduct:** refused to throw good money after bad (SsangYong); exits of ~15 businesses
